posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

Where did the antimatter go? The Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other instantly. So why does anything exist at all? Scientists are still hunting for the missing half of reality.

What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. But thanks to new techniques for DNA sequencing, dating ancient detritus, mathematical models, and aerial and lidar archaeology, we are now able to get a faint idea of what this world might have looked and felt like.

Autumn really knows how to show off 🍁⁠
⁠
@motaz_azaiza captured the season from above, where every tree turns its own shade of red, orange, gold, or green, and quiet roads wind through the colors.⁠
⁠
Which slide is your favorite? ⁠

German photographer Christian Vieler, who is world-renowned for his dog photography, turned his camera to senior dogs, and the result is pure warmth. ⁠
⁠
Each portrait shows a dog who has slowed down a little but hasn’t lost any of their spark. ⁠
⁠⁠
Which photo is your favorite?!⁠

A bar where you get great beer and a few slaps and kicks from the Muscle Girls? 🍺😂 ⁠
This unusual experience combines a night out with some playful sparring from strong women, making it a bar visit you definitely won’t forget.⁠
⁠
Would you try it, or stick to just the beer? 👀⁠
🎥: @ngtnz

Harry Potter fans know this bridge as the route to Hogwarts, but the Glenfinnan Viaduct was carrying trains across the Scottish Highlands long before the films. ⁠
⁠
Opened in 1901, it was built from mass concrete with no steel inside, and its 21 arches stretch about 381 meters above the River Finnan.⁠
⁠
Every year from June to October, the Jacobite steam train travels between Fort William and Mallaig, crossing the viaduct along the way. ⁠
⁠
You don’t need a ticket to see it: the trails near the
Comment HOTEL and I’ll send you the list - including the decision maker’s name and email for each one.

Have you ever seen a bird with sunflower-like eyes? 🌻⁠
⁠
These birds are white-crested Helmetshrikes, and that bright yellow “sunflower” is actually a skin structure called a wattle that only adults have.⁠
⁠
They are as social as they are striking. They live in close-knit groups that can stay together for years, and the whole group helps raise the chicks.⁠
⁠
By: @veronicadonoso_b

No traffic lights, no problem! ⁠
In Thimphu, the capital of Bhutan, traffic is directed by police officers using hand signals from a small decorative booth instead of automated lights. 🚦⁠
⁠
The city once tried traffic lights, but they were eventually removed in favor of human traffic control. A unique sight that makes you look twice when exploring Bhutan!⁠
🎥: @thecubancarrie

Artist @simonorourke turned a storm-damaged tree into a giant hand reaching for the sky.⁠
⁠
Once the tallest tree in Wales, it was due to be cut down after a storm left it damaged. ⁠
⁠
Simon turned it into a memorial for the much-loved landmark, known as "Giant Hand of Vyrnwy."⁠
⁠

@amiina_abroad discovers a restaurant in Thailand where getting through the entrance can save you money! 😂⁠
⁠
The restaurant has different-sized gates, and the one you manage to squeeze through determines your discount, ranging from 5% to 20%. A pretty unusual way to welcome customers and add a little challenge before the meal even begins! 🍜👀⁠
⁠
Which gate do you think you’d make it through?

Your bucket list just got a little longer 🌍

These are some of the most breathtaking places on Earth worth visiting at least once!

Which one is already on your list? ⁠
⁠
By: @leina.sevele @lifeofawaterphotographer @globetrottingcom @hobopeeba Aylin Çıplak

Vietnamese street food always finds a way to surprise you! 🇻🇳🍗⁠
One cooking method that might catch your eye is chicken roasted upright over a beer can, using the can to help keep the meat moist while it cooks. The result is golden, juicy chicken with crispy skin and plenty of flavor.⁠
⁠
This is definitely one for the curious food lovers! 🤤⁠
Would you try chicken cooked this way?⁠
🎥: @chopsticktravel

The scale of Western Australia's mines is hard to grasp until you see them from the air. ⁠
⁠
Some tailings ponds stretch 4 km or more across the outback, and the open-cut nickel and gold mines are so large they look like meteor craters...or paintings, you decide!⁠
⁠
By: @scottjonphotography
